source.title: The Neural Tangent Kernel in High Dimensions: Triple Descent and a Multi-Scale Theory of Generalization

record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes test error across parameter and data scales using high-dimensional NTK kernel regression and finite single-hidden-layer networks, and reports evidence of multiple descents. This is a different method and setting from the original claim, while refining its simple double-descent account.
record.gate_note: The text reports test-error outcomes for parameter-width sweeps and data-size learning curves, including finite-network experiments. Results cited from other studies are not recorded. Plot settings and parameter values used to generate figures are not treated as separate outcomes.
record.test_reason: The study gives exact asymptotic test-error curves for NTK ridge regression and runs finite-size experiments, including a single-hidden-layer net trained with gradient descent. Its results argue that simple double descent is incomplete. There is extra non-monotonicity at p≈m², a spike in feature count, and SNR-dependent sample-wise humps. This is a different method (T2) whose explicit aim is to show that the double-descent picture needs restating (T5).
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors conclude that NTK regression test error is non-monotonic deep in the overparameterized regime, with extra peaks when p scales quadratically with m. Double descent is therefore not always accurate or complete. They attribute the quadratic-scale non-monotonicity to the second-layer kernel K2, and conjecture that the multi-scale behaviour extends to broader architectures.
record.recipe_differences: The study combines high-dimensional asymptotic analysis of NTK kernel ridge regression with finite-size experiments on single-hidden-layer networks, rather than the original studies' settings and procedures.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported behavior varies with parameterization scale, feature count, SNR, initialization variance σW², and centering. The authors also report qualitative differences between NTK regression and gradient-descent dynamics.
record.problems: The theoretical setting is restricted to a single-hidden-layer fully connected network, Gaussian inputs, and a wide teacher network. The finite experiments use specified synthetic settings; numerical curve values are generally presented in figures rather than stated in text. Epoch-wise double descent and optimally tuned regularization are not tested.

untested.parts: Deep (multi-layer) networks and real datasets; only a single-hidden-layer net on Gaussian synthetic data is tested.
Entire version; the predictor is taken at t→∞.
Neural networks trained by gradient descent and real data; only NTK kernel regression learning curves are tested.
Whether the peaks disappear under optimally tuned ridge regularization; γ is fixed small or zero.
Model classes other than NTK and random-feature kernel regression and a single-hidden-layer net.

missing.what: High-SNR and noiseless learning curves showing no sample-wise humps; error decreases as m^-2 without noise and as m^-1 with noise.
Comparison of centered and uncentered loss: centering, which removes initialization variance, markedly lowers loss at large n1.
Theoretical predictions agree with empirical kernel regression near n1≈m.

record.verdict_notes: Most rows are NTK or random-feature kernel regression, so V1 (deep networks) is linked only to the GD-trained shallow net (r10). Triple descent appears even with zero label noise (Fig. 4a, 4c), so the peaks here come from initialization or feature variance rather than label noise alone. That is consistent with V6's 'or variance' wording. Ridge γ is fixed (10^-3, 10^-6 or 0), so optimal regularization is untested.

versions.untested_parts: Other architectures and data-generating settings beyond the studied single-hidden-layer networks and Gaussian-input teacher setup.
No test-error sweep over training epochs or training time is reported; the kernel predictor is defined at t→∞.
The reported data-size effect is for the studied NTK setting and signal-to-noise conditions, not a broad sweep across architectures or datasets.
Broad model classes beyond NTK regression, random-feature limits, and the studied single-hidden-layer networks.
The study does not test whether one measure of effective complexity predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.
The study varies signal-to-noise ratio and initialization variance and reports multiple peaks, but does not test whether peaks disappear under optimally tuned regularization.
The study does not recast complexity using an effective parameter count to test whether the second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: Second-layer kernel K2 (NTK ridge regression)
rows.operation_detail: Varied parameter count by changing network width and measured test loss.
rows.measure: Test loss as a function of parameter count
rows.value: Non-monotonic behavior is clearly visible at the linear scaling transition p = m.
rows.note: The study describes a sharp rise near the interpolation threshold followed by a quick descent as p increases further. Numerical curve values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: Second-layer random-feature kernel (asymptotic theory), not a deep network, so V1 does not apply. It shows only the single linear-transition peak, so it is not evidence of multiple peaks for V6. The value is theoretical, not empirical.

rows.subject: Full NTK K (NTK ridge regression)
rows.operation_detail: Varied parameter count by changing network width and measured test loss.
rows.measure: Test loss as a function of parameter count
rows.value: Non-monotonic behavior is clearly visible at the quadratic scaling transition p = m².
rows.note: The authors describe a second transition near p = m², with further non-monotonic behavior. Numerical curve values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: Full-NTK kernel regression (theory), not a deep network; drop V1.

rows.subject: Full NTK (NTK regression)
rows.operation_detail: Jointly varied feature count n0 and hidden width n1 and measured test error.
rows.measure: Test error over n0/m and n1/m
rows.value: For fixed φ, test error has a hump near n1 = m; at large n1 it also has a spike near n0 = m. The feature-count non-monotonicity disappears for small n1.
rows.note: The text explicitly describes both the width-related hump and feature-count spike, and states that the latter is absent at small n1.
rows.check: Kernel regression theory; drop V1. The feature-count spike appears only at large n1.

source_check.locator_found: Figure 3(a), caption; Section 7, paragraph describing joint feature and width variation.

rows.subject: Full NTK (NTK regression)
rows.operation_detail: Varied dataset size and measured test error learning curves.

conditions.value: Small enough SNR; multiple SNR curves shown

rows.measure: Test error as a function of training-set size
rows.value: For small enough SNR, visible bumps near m = n0 and m = n1 show regimes where more training data hurts test performance.
rows.note: The study says the two humps occur at sample-size transitions; it does not give a numerical SNR threshold in the text.
rows.check: Observed only for small enough SNR. The noiseless curve shows no humps and is not recorded.

rows.subject: Full NTK (NTK regression)
rows.operation_detail: Changed σW² to vary the relative contributions of per-layer kernels K1 and K2.
rows.measure: Test error as a function of width
rows.value: As σW² decreases and the kernel becomes more like K2, the small hump at the quadratic transition increases until it resembles the large spike at the linear transition.
rows.note: The authors infer from this component-variation comparison that K2 is responsible for non-monotonicity in the quadratically overparameterized regime.
rows.check: σW² is the initialization variance of the second layer, not a regularization strength. The row bears on the multiple-peak part of V6 only.

source_check.correct: Figure 3(c): tanh activation; decreasing second-layer initialization variance increases the quadratic-transition hump as the kernel approaches K2. Ridge parameter γ is not stated for this panel; γ=0 is specified for Figure 3(a).
source_check.problem: The stated γ=0 condition is not established for Figure 3(c).

rows.value: The global minimum need not be at n1 = ∞; for this configuration the optimal parameter count lies between m and m², and the curves show a peak near the linear transition and a bump near the quadratic transition.
